en: Abdulla Qodiriy and the Birth of the Uzbek Novel

intro.uz: Biografik-akademik matn: oʻzbek romanchiligining asoschisi Abdulla Qodiriy hayoti va ijodi. Topshiriqlar: True/False/Not Given, test savollari (muallif maqsadi, asosiy fikr) va gap toʻldirish. Taxminan 20 daqiqa ajrating: avval matnni tez koʻrib chiqib har bir xatboshining mavzusini belgilang, keyin TFNG savollarida sanalar va «first», «only», «of his own free will» kabi soʻzlarga alohida eʼtibor bering — aynan ular javobni hal qiladi.

paragraphs.en: Few writers occupy a position in their national literature comparable to the one Abdulla Qodiriy holds in Uzbek letters. Born in Tashkent in 1894, he lived through one of the most turbulent periods in the history of Central Asia, witnessing the final decades of Russian imperial administration, the upheavals of revolution and civil war, and the consolidation of Soviet power. His reputation rests chiefly on a single book, Oʻtkan kunlar, usually rendered in English as Days Gone By, which is widely regarded as the first Uzbek novel. Yet to treat him simply as the author of one celebrated work would be to underestimate both the range of his writing and the extent of his influence.

Qodiriy came of age at a time when educated circles in Turkestan were engaged in intense debate about how their society should respond to modernity. Reform-minded intellectuals, often referred to as the Jadids, argued for new methods of schooling, a revitalised press and a literature capable of addressing contemporary problems. Qodiriy, who had received both a traditional education and some schooling of a more modern kind, is generally associated with this current of thought. His early career was devoted largely to journalism, and he became known for satirical sketches in which the pretensions of officials and the absurdities of everyday life were exposed with considerable wit.

Days Gone By first appeared in instalments in the early 1920s before being published as a complete book in the middle of the decade. Set in the mid-nineteenth century, principally in Tashkent and Margilan, the novel follows the love of Otabek, a young Tashkent merchant, for Kumush, a girl from Margilan. Their happiness, however, is repeatedly threatened, not only by the intrigues of rivals but by the social conventions of the day. Pressed by his family into a second marriage, Otabek finds himself trapped in a household where jealousy eventually leads to tragedy. Around this private drama the author weaves a wider picture of a society weakened by factional feuds and corrupt officials, a society that, the novel implies, contributed to its own decline.

What made the novel so striking to its first readers was less its plot than its manner. Much earlier prose in the region, critics have observed, had tended towards didactic tales and ornate, formulaic description, whereas Qodiriy offered characters with recognisable inner lives, whose motives were revealed gradually through dialogue and action. His language, too, marked a departure: rather than relying on the elevated vocabulary of classical literature, he drew extensively on the spoken Uzbek of his time, giving his narrative an immediacy that readers had seldom encountered on the page. It is this combination of psychological depth and vernacular vitality that critics most often cite when explaining why the book has never lost its readership.

Qodiriy's second novel, Mehrobdan chayon, which may be translated as The Scorpion from the Altar, appeared towards the end of the 1920s. Set in the Kokand Khanate, it is again built around a love story, but its satirical edge is sharper. The title itself points to the novel's central concern: hypocrisy concealed behind a façade of piety and authority. Through its portrait of scheming courtiers and self-serving clerics, the book develops the critique of power that had been present in his earlier work, while confirming his mastery of the historical novel as a vehicle for reflecting on the present.

His career was cut short in the most brutal manner. During the wave of mass repression that swept the Soviet Union in the late 1930s, Qodiriy was arrested, and in 1938 he was executed, sharing the fate of many other prominent Uzbek writers and thinkers of his generation. For a considerable time afterwards, his name could scarcely be mentioned in public, and his books were removed from circulation. Only after Stalin's death was he officially rehabilitated, and it was not until later still that his novels gradually regained the place they now occupy in schools and libraries.

Qodiriy's legacy is visible throughout modern Uzbek prose. Later novelists who turned to the past in order to explore questions of identity, morality and national memory worked, consciously or not, within a tradition he had established. Days Gone By has been adapted for stage and screen, and its characters remain familiar to a wide public. Perhaps the most telling measure of his achievement, however, is that readers continue to approach his work not as a historical curiosity but as living literature, finding in its portrayal of love, ambition and social pressure concerns that remain recognisably their own.

grammar.example: which is widely regarded as the first Uzbek novel

questions.statement: Qodiriy was born in a city that is also one of the main settings of Days Gone By.

explain.uz: A: «Born in Tashkent in 1894»; C: roman «principally in Tashkent and Margilan» da kechadi. Ikki maʼlumotni bogʻlab xulosa chiqariladi.

questions.statement: Qodiriy studied abroad before beginning his career as a journalist.

explain.uz: B xatboshida u anʼanaviy va zamonaviyroq taʼlim olgani aytilgan, lekin chet elda oʻqigani haqida hech narsa yoʻq.

questions.statement: Days Gone By was originally released as a single complete volume.

explain.uz: «first appeared in instalments in the early 1920s before being published as a complete book» — avval qismlarga boʻlib chop etilgan.

questions.statement: Otabek enters his second marriage of his own free will.

explain.uz: «Pressed by his family into a second marriage» — oila bosimi bilan, oʻz xohishi bilan emas.

questions.statement: The novel suggests that internal divisions played a part in the decline of the society it depicts.

explain.uz: «a society weakened by factional feuds … contributed to its own decline» — «internal divisions» = «factional feuds».

questions.statement: Mehrobdan chayon sold more copies than Days Gone By in the 1920s.

explain.uz: Ikkinchi roman mavzusi va uslubi tasvirlangan, ammo sotuv yoki tiraj haqida maʼlumot yoʻq.

questions.statement: Qodiriy was officially rehabilitated while Stalin was still alive.

explain.uz: «Only after Stalin's death was he officially rehabilitated» — Stalin vafotidan keyin.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main purpose in the final sentence of paragraph A?
options: to suggest that Days Gone By has been overrated
to indicate that Qodiriy's importance goes beyond one famous novel
to explain why Qodiriy wrote so little
to compare Qodiriy with writers from other countries

explain.uz: «to treat him simply as the author of one celebrated work would be to underestimate both the range of his writing and the extent of his influence» — matn uning boshqa asarlari va taʼsirini ham koʻrib chiqadi.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph D, what most distinguished Qodiriy's novel from earlier prose?
options: its unusually dramatic and complicated plot
its use of the elevated vocabulary of classical literature
its psychologically convincing characters and use of everyday speech
its clear moral lessons for young readers

explain.uz: «characters with recognisable inner lives» va «drew extensively on the spoken Uzbek of his time». Klassik leksika — aksincha, undan voz kechgan; syujet esa «less its plot than its manner».

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what does the title Mehrobdan chayon point to?
options: dishonesty hidden behind religious and political respectability
the decline of trade in the Kokand Khanate

explain.uz: «hypocrisy concealed behind a façade of piety and authority» — «hypocrisy» = dishonesty, «piety and authority» = religious and political respectability.

questions.prompt: What does the writer consider the strongest evidence of Qodiriy's achievement?
options: the adaptation of his novel for stage and screen
the number of later novelists who imitated him
the fact that readers still find his work personally relevant
the inclusion of his books in school programmes

explain.uz: «Perhaps the most telling measure of his achievement … is that readers continue to approach his work … as living literature». Boshqa variantlar tilga olingan, lekin «eng muhim oʻlchov» sifatida emas.

questions.prompt: Before he became a novelist, Qodiriy was known for ___ that mocked the pretensions of officials.

explain.uz: «he became known for satirical sketches in which the pretensions of officials … were exposed».

questions.prompt: Instead of classical vocabulary, Qodiriy drew on the ___ of his time.

explain.uz: «he drew extensively on the spoken Uzbek of his time».

questions.prompt: In the novel, ___ within Otabek's household finally results in tragedy.

explain.uz: «a household where jealousy eventually leads to tragedy» — «results in» = «leads to».
